subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF FARMERS IN OKANAGAN-SIMILKAMEEN, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, farmers in Okanagan-Similkameen have reason to feel unjustly put upon. Economically many who may not survive the winter can only wonder at the Government's failure to act in their defence. Now farmers find that the very structure of their industry is under attack, perhaps being destroyed by federal government action under the Combines Investigation Act.
One industry official told the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), "We have been operating this system for nearly 50 years. If we have been doing something wrong, tell us and we will correct it, but don't take action which will cost us hundreds of thousands of dollars to defend. We are in deep financial trouble without that."
To discourage farmers in the area further, the CBC reported in a most inflammatory manner alleging racial bias, intolerance, and harassment of orchard workers, in generalized statements which are condemned and challenged by the industry.
A further series of unworthy statements made to the Special Committee on Visible Minorities on behalf of transient workers from Quebec is so overstated as to cause despair on the part of the vast majority of Okanagan farmers who are decent and fair in their relationships with their labour.
It is a sad day when a farmer, receiving five cents for a product which costs him 13 cents to produce, and who is paying the highest farm wages in all of Canada, should be subjected to the kind of abuse which seems to be thrown at him by Government, CBC and individuals with an axe to grind.

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF INDEXING TO TOBACCO PRODUCTS- ESTABLISHMENT OF TASK FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 notice that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has announced a task force to examine the current method of indexing the excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco products, chaired by Dr. Douglas Peters. He states that the task force is being established in response to industry's concerns about the technical operation of the indexing system. Surely the word "industry" includes the tobacco-growing industry. This is the industry the Government is systematically setting out to destroy, and that destruction must stop.
The recent 15.8 per cent increase in federal tax on cigarettes is totally unacceptable, and the provincial ad valorem tax in Ontario on top of that is unbearable. The federal Government alone took in $1.14 billion in tax on tobacco last year when the market value to growers was only some $285 million, a four to one ratio. The task force, indeed, has a serious task, that is, to reverse this government rip-off of the agricultural sector.
I note that individuals and associations are asked to make submissions to the task force and to send them to Dr. Peters at the Department of Finance. I would call on any one in this country who is concerned about the Government's abuse of agriculture to make such a submission to Dr. Peters.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF RESEARCH STATION ON COLONY FARM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Colony Farm is the last large farm left on the north shore of the Fraser River, in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia, near metro Vancouver. This 800 acre farm is owned by the British Columbia Government. That Government now wishes to privatize it and sell it to developers so that it can be blacktopped.
Action has been taken at the community level to save this farm. The reason 1 raise this issue in the House of Commons is that representation has also been made to the federal Minister of Agriculture, asking him to set up an agricultural research station on the farm.
In light of the quickly disappearing farmland in the country, and particularly in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia, and in light of the fact that today the livestock from that farm is going up for sale, and that we do need agricultural research facilities in the area, I urge the Minister of Agriculture to enter into negotiations with the Province either to purchase the land itself, or to buy the land in conjunction with the University of British Columbia.
The matter is urgent, and the Minister will be pressed next week by the former Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody and by the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett). I urge the Minister of Agriculture to act on this right away if he does not want to lose his green hat.

subsubtopic: THE CASE OF HUGH HAMBLETON-EMPLOYMENT WITH CIDA- REQUESTS FOR INFORMATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I have a number of questions to ask. Why is the Government blocking questions regarding Hugh Hambleton, the Canadian spy who worked in the NATO Secretariat in Paris, in Peru and Haiti ostensibly for CIDA, but in reality on behalf of the KGB? Who is being protected? Why is the Government attempting to prevent all of the truth from coming out?
The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) tells me that the case is closed as far as he is concerned. The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) tells me that he is in no position to comment on the matter. How can the case be closed when we do not yet know who in the Government granted Hambleton immunity although he was known to be a spy? We do not know who warned him not to go to Britain where, as he was told, he was certain to be tried on charges of espionage. Who tipped him off in Britain before he went through the immigration line by suggesting that it would be in his interest to return to Canada? Who is covering up these traces of espionage?
November 25, 1983
Who recommended Mr. Hambleton for a ranking position in CIDA as soon as he had joined that organization and had been sent off to Peru? Perhaps most important of all, given all of the things that were known by early 1982 about his work on behalf of the KGB, why was he not brought to trial in Canada? Was he delivered up to the British authorities because a trial in Canada would have brought out some unpleasant home truths?

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REMOVAL OF TAX ON FARM FUELS AND FERTILIZERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Government cannot begin to make up for all of the damage it has caused Canadian farmers through its ridiculous policies. However, it has a responsibility at the very least to remove the federal tax on farm fuels and fertilizers.
Let us look at the Government's record on agriculture. It has refused to provide the Farm Credit Corporation with enough money to keep Canadian farmers afloat. It has forced the Western Grain Transportation Act through without regard for those who must bear the financial burden, namely, the western Canadian farmers. The Government agreed to consider changes in the Western Grain Stabilization Act only after many farmers had gone bankrupt waiting for long overdue changes to be implemented. Those changes have not even occurred as yet.
New statistics show that 390 Canadian farmers went bankrupt between January and October 31 of this year. In my home Province of Manitoba, nearly twice as many farmers have gone bankrupt so far this year as compared to the same period last year. That is absolutely unacceptable.
It should be reasonable to expect the Government at least to aid farmers by dropping the federal tax on farm fuels and fertilizers. This gesture could be the first step toward loosening the financial stranglehold in which the Liberal Government has placed thousands of Canadian farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I disagree, certainly to some extent, with the concluding part of the Hon. Member's question. There has been a continuous drop in the unemployment rate over the last seven months. If he looks at the employment figures rather than the unemployment figures, he knows there has been an increase in permanent jobs in the Canadian economy of well over 300,000 since last autumn. I do not think the picture is as bleak as his citation of the figures would show. Clearly there is great room for improvement on the unemployment side, and that is the focus of the policies of this Government.
In reply to the first part of his question, I would say the increase in profits reflects the extraordinary low level they were at before and I would have thought he would be rejoicing at the existence of those profits, since those profits and their reinvestment in the economy are the source of the creation of jobs in the economy. It is something we should be pleased about and not something which the Hon. Member appears to regret.

As to the Government's theory on the way to get a recovery, if increased profits are supposed to lead to new investment and produce jobs, why have two different agencies, one government, and one private, said it is not working? The Conference Board of Canada said that for 1983 investment is going to be down by more than 10 per cent, while profits have gone up by 92 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the House the fact that yesterday Graham Spry passed away. He was 83 years old and died peacefully.

November 25, 1983
The Late Graham Spry
Mr. Spry was a reporter, war correspondent, scholar, lobbyist and Canadian par excellence. His Canadian Radio League in the early 1930s pushed for a public broadcasting network in Canada and Parliament created the CBC in 1936. That is why Mr. Spry was called the father of the CBC. He was also one of the founders of the CCF and was an assistant to Sir Stafford Cripps. Mr. Spry leaves behind his wife Irene, herself a distinguished economist and historian, and a son and a daughter.
Mr. Spry even stood for this House a number of times and in his own words was always defeated by large and enthusiastic majorities! Yet he still offered to Canada his ideas and his visions of a united federal Canada through communications. Those ideas and visions were adopted by all three Parties which are presently in the House.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, he was a journalist and a man of great depth, and we shall miss his vision and his ideas.

Perhaps I may conclude by saying that 1 had the honour to meet Mr. Spry when he was 80 years old and it was a great privilege for me. I could see that sparkle in his eyes. He was a humble man yet he had done so much for Canada. He was truly a great Canadian who had given a great deal to my generation. 1 believe that the generation to come, although they will never know him personally, will be the beneficiaries of his ideas, of the CBC and of some of his other accomplishments in the area of broadcasting in Canada. During his 83 years he contributed immensely to Canada. He was really a great Canadian and we will miss him.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Vancouv-er-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) for the excellent idea of taking notice of this sad and important event, an event which is especially sad for the family of Graham Spry. 1 am one of those who had the privilege to know Mr. Spry, although from somewhat of a distance. As a young man, 1 knew what he had done because I lived in an isolated rural community in the Province of New Brunswick. I realized very early that the radio broadcasts of which he was very much one of the founding fathers had linked Canadian communities and Canadian people in ways which were not always as visible as this institution but which were no less real.

I think that in the history of our country, we shall have reason to remember people like Graham Spry. I know that his desire to see a greater understanding among Canadians made him choose this form of transmitting the information and knowledge that form the sole basis for understanding and tolerance among people who, historically have differed in origin, language and beliefs.

I believe this country will survive not only because of its wealth but because of its citizens. Graham Spry sensed a very
long time ago that understanding and tolerance would come from knowledge, and that broadcasting could transmit that knowledge. In every sense of the word, Graham Spry was a father of the new Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with those who have already spoken in tribute to the late Graham Spry. I am particularly pleased to be able to speak in tribute to this man as Graham Spry, among his many other accomplishments, was a good and faithful servant of the Province of Saskatchewan for many years. He served as Agent General in the Ofifce of the Province of Saskatchewan in London.
One of the things that I most particularly recall about Graham Spry, not knowing him personally but knowing of him and his family and the distinction with which all of them have served our country, was his love for the Gatineau Hills. He had a residence in the Gatineau Hills where he spent many, many hours of his life. I know he spent those hours with the greatest of enjoyment, as many of us have had the privilege and pleasure of doing the same.
As has been pointed out, he was a distinguished citizen of the country and a Companion of the Order of Canada. He was a recipient of the John Drainie Award in 1972 for his distinguished contribution to broadcasting. He will be sorely missed by all Canadians because of his contributions and I know that I speak on behalf of ail Members of the House when I extend to his widow and his children our sincere and heartfelt condolences.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-172 proposes certain amendments to the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act. This legislation, which was passed by Parliament many months ago, provided, as a last resort, financial aid to older workers affected by permanent lay-offs in designated industrial sectors or communities in Canada. The sectors in question could be designated either nationally, regionally or locally. Industries designated at the national level include textiles, clothing, footwear and leather. As the House is aware, these sectors are experiencing major economic problems as result of competition from imports and industrial restructuring. At the end of September, we had 2,080 active files under this program. Sixteen more communities and a number of other industries were also designated under the Industrial and Labour Adjustment Program. At the present time, 321 people are receiving assistance under the program which comes under the Labour Adjustment Benefits Act.
The amendments to Bill C-78 as proposed in Bill C-172 are the results of presentations made by Members on both sides of the House, by union representatives, especially the CSD, and by employers and private citizens.
I am happy today to be able to act on the representations I received. First of all, the proposed amendments will prevent involuntary deductions from survivor's pensions when benefits are calculated. Many widows and widowers were being treated unfairly under the present legislation, which was clearly not the intention of the legislator.
Second, the amendments proposed in Bill C-172 will also provide greater flexibility in eligibility criteria for workers less than fifty-four years of age, with many years of service, who will now be able to take advantage of their combined years of service in designated sectors. It was pointed out to us, more specifically, that it was unfair that someone who had worked for thirty years in the textile industry could be eligible for benefits while a neighbour with twenty years of experience in the textile industry and twenty years in the clothing industry,

November 25, 1983
Labour Adjustment Benefits Act would not be eligible because he did not have thirty years of employment in the same sector. We are therefore introducing a remedy that will allow workers to combine their years of service in sectors designated for the purposes of this legislation.
Third, the amendments will resolve a problem of interpretation, owing to the different definitions of "lay off" in English and in French, by eliminating the word "involuntary" from the English version.
Fourth, the bill will provide for payment of benefits to qualified workers whose applications for certification to the Labour Adjustment Review Board were delayed for reasons beyond their control. There is always a possibility of administrative delay, and 1 think it would be unfair to blame such delays on the person who is supposed to receive these benefits. Therefore an anormaly in the Act will be corrected in order to deal fairly with potential, qualified recipients.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to remind Hon. Members just how important it is to adopt these amendments without delay. I thank all my colleagues on this side of the House as well as the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party for agreeing to adopt this Bill today because, as many of us know, Quebec's National Assembly amended its pension plan last June, making it possible for workers, among other things, to retire at age 60 with appropriate actuarial adjustments. want to thank the union representatives who made representations and submitted a well-researched brief to my Department.
It enabled us to draft the amendments which we are introducing today and which will certainly be a definite advantage to Canadian workers eligible for those adjustment benefits.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: GARNISHMENT, ATTACHMENT AND PENSION DIVERSION ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, His Excellency the Governor General has been informed of the purport of this Bill and has given his consent, as far as Her Majesty's prerogatives are affected, to the consideration by Parliament of the Bill, that Parliament may do therein as it thinks fit.
Most Hon. Members, Mr. Speaker, will be aware of the controversy which has arisen over whether or not the wording of the Garnishment, Attachment and Pension Diversion Act includes Members of Parliament as well as the staff of the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library of Parliament.

Last September, the Seventh Small Claims Court of Ottawa-Carleton considered a case involving a member of the staff of the House of Commons. In its decision rendered in mid-October, the Court stated that the Act in question applies to the staff of the House of Commons. The amount due was determined last Monday and the employee concerned has appealed the decision of the Small Claims Court.

While I am satisfied that the appellate courts would uphold the lower court decision, the appeal process would likely be a lengthy one. Such a delay would not, in my view, be fair to spouses seeking to enforce family support orders, not to other types of creditors. For this reason I am proposing amendments which make it abundantly clear that Members of Parliament, from both the upper and lower Houses, and the staff of the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library of Parliament, are subject to garnishment under the Garnishment, Attachment and Pension Diversion Act. This will be achieved by creating a separate division to apply to the House of Commons, the Senate and the Library of Parliament.
Once the Act has passed, the necessary regulations will go forward to the Governor in Council as soon as the Speakers of the House of Commons and the Senate have indicated their approval of the regulations to me. This will clear the way for the regulations for the pension diversion portions of the Act which have been delayed pending clarification of Part I. It will clear the way for them to proceed and be proclaimed into force early in January, 1984.
I would just say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that this is not, as is quite evident from the consent here this morning, a partisan matter. It is equally important, I think, to all of us in the House of Commons that we be seen not to be obstructing in any way legislation which was passed last year and in which we believed we had already yielded this ancient privilege. As a result of the delays which have occurred, litigants are in danger of being put to great expense in achieving what we thought had already been guaranteed by the law.
This is, therefore, a clarificatory piece of legislation. It may not be strictly necessary in terms of law. In fact, I do not believe it is; but certainly it is necessary in terms of fact so that Parliament will not be seen to be holding on in an unseemly way to privileges which it has already assured the public it has abandoned.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak very briefly to this Bill. I just wanted to say a couple of things with respect to the amendments which Members of our Party will, of course, support. As the Minister himself pointed out in September of this year, it has been an unedifying spectacle that the very important Parts II, III and IV of the Bill have not as yet been proclaimed.
The intention was at the time the Bill originally came before the House that the matter be put into effect immediately. Indeed, Members of our Party have been calling for this legislation for some considerable period of time. I recall in 1980 a former colleague from Leeds-Grenville, Mr. Tom Cossitt, was very active in asking for this legislation to be brought forward. It continued to be the case on the part of my colleague from Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), who in fact raised this matter with the Minister in September of this year. He should be given some credit for really bringing this matter to the point where the Minister has, to his credit, brought forward the amending legislation. I am sure there will be no question as to the right to effect garnishee and other action of attachment with respect to Members and staff of the House of Commons, the Senate, and the Library of Parliament.
I will pose a specific question now and ask the Ministr during Committee of the Whole to comment on this aspect of the Bill. There is a unique provision, as I pointed out to the Minister earlier, on which he may wish to comment. Under clause 16(2) it is specifically provided that there shall be no execution against the House of Commons and the Senate in respect of a garnishment served on a Member of the House of Commons, a staff member of whomever, or the Senate. I would appreciate hearing the legal rationale for that particular provision.
The effect, as I would understand it, would be that if the House of Commons, for example, did not obey the garnishment order, it would not be possible for litigants to proceed to execution against the House of Commons and to receive the money that they would be entitled to under the judgment. I am sure the Minister has had an opportunity to obtain a legal opinion or advice with respect to that provision. I would be
November 25, 1983

obliged, accordingly, if he would answer that point during the course of the Committee of the Whole.
In conclusion, all I can say is that we are in support of these amendments. We are very anxious that the rights apply, particularly in cases of those maintenance orders and orders for single parents that are very often difficult to enforce for a variety of reasons in our federal state. When these orders are extant and in fact involve public employees, or indeed Members of the House of Commons or the Senate, our Party believes that the same rights apply in the enforcement of such debts against all citizens of Canada. Hence, we have no difficulty with the relinquishment of what have been traditional rights or exemption from garnishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to this Bill on behalf of the New Democratic Party. As I understand Bill C-171, it is essentially a housekeeping measure. The amendments are proposed to tighten up the poor drafting of the original Bill, Bill C-38, which was passed on June 18, 1982. Although it has taken a year and a half to correct the vagueness of Bill C-38, we must commend the Government for recognizing this and acting upon it. We will support Bill C-171.
As the Minister said, some of the ambiguities in the present Bill were revealed in a recent court case. For the record, the case was Texaco Canada Limited versus Dagenais. It was a decision of the Small Claims Court in Ontario on October 12, 1983. This subsequent scrutiny of the Bill indicated that there was some doubt as to whether MPs and Senators would have been included in the original Bill as well as Parliament Hill employees. Clearly, the principle is that we should all be equal under the law. That is the motto of the Supreme Court of the United States and I believe it applies equally in Canada. Therefore, the lawmakers and employees on the Hill should not be above the law either.
There are three principles in the original Bill C-38 on which I would like to comment. The first principle is that Bill C-38 eliminated a form of privilege which is that the wages of the employees of the Crown were exempt from garnishment based on the historic concept of royal prerogative, which holds that since a court cannot move binding orders against the moneys and properties of Her Majesty, a garnishment order cannot be made against money paid by the Crown to an employee of the Crown. There was no just reason for these categories of people to be afforded special treatment. Personally, I had a case with one of my constituents in Vancouver who was trying to collect money from her former husband on a maintenance order. She could not garnishee his wages because he was an employee of the Crown. This was cleared up in the old Bill.
I suggest that we should acknowledge the support of the Public Service Alliance of Canada of Bill C-38. They acknowledged that federal employees should not be able to hide behind their debts.
I think we should also give credit to Parliament Hill employees who appreciate the clarifying aspects of Bill C-171. While they recognize that they should not have special status,
Garnishment, Attachment and Pension Diversion Act I want to point out to the Minister that, on the other hand, they should not be subject to special handicaps or exemptions. While we do not want to give them the special privileges which are eliminated in this Bill, they do not have the equal privilege of collective bargaining and organizing. In other words, we do not treat the employees of Parliament Hill equally. If we are to apply the principle of having their wages subject to garnishment like the rest of the population, the principle equally applies that they should be allowed to collectively organize, receive decent salaries and be able to bargain for their working conditions. Let us be fair and apply the principles right across the board. I am sure the Minister would agree that the same principle of equality must apply.
The second principle in the original Bill corrected the unfairness to creditors. People should not be able to abdicate their financial responsibilities simply because they are Crown employees. I believe we all agree with that.
Third, the original Bill allowed the Government to divert pension benefits to comply with financial support orders. This provision is contained in Part II of Bill C-38 and has yet to come into effect. We urge the Government to fix a date of proclamation for the remaining elements of Bill C-38, Parts II to IV. 1 believe the Conservative Party spokesman, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), made reference to this. What is the Minister waiting for? Why does he not proclaim those particular sections?
We in the NDP are in full agreement with the exemption of Old Age Security and veteran war disability pensions from those diversion provisions as covered by Bill C-38.
In summary, we are glad to see the original legislation improved upon and the intent clarified before the end of the session. On a personal note, I just lost a rather large legal case which I have fought for three years all the way to the Supreme Court of Canada. It took eight days in the trial division in British Columbia. I do not know whether the Minister will garnish my wages to collect his legal costs. Perhaps I might in fact be one of the first people to which this Bill applies. Perhaps I will have to appeal it, win against him in the appeal court and then garnishee his wages!
In conclusion, we on this side of the House support the speedy passage of this legislation. However, I remind the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) that if he is going to rely on the principle of equality, not only must Parliament Hill employees suffer the consequences of having their wages garnisheed and so on like anyone else, but they should be equally treated to some of the benefits of the general population, to wit, the right to collectively bargain.

Certainly we do not object to that. Also we understand that it is without prejudice to their right to give notice of any objection to any item in the Supplementary Estimates before it is really five o clock.
November 25, 1983

I do not know whether I have covered all the concerns of the Hon. Member but certainly, Mr. Speaker, if you call it five o'clock now, we will agree without prejudice to what I have just said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

Accordingly, I appreciate that clarification. I understand that there may be a reasonable number of objections which are now in the process of scrutiny and preparation, and that we will retain the ability to file not only the content of our Opposition
Business of the House
motion but, indeed, the notices of objections before five o'clock Eastern Standard Time, Canada.

On behalf of the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to co-operate in calling it five o'clock for many reasons. One, of course, is that we do have many Members from British Columbia who are busily preparing for the impending B.C. Lions victory by two touchdowns over the Toronto Argonauts!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Subject to the conditions mentioned by the Hon. Member, the President of the Privy Council and the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West, is it the pleasure of the House that I call it five o'clock?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Accordingly, I extend best wishes for a pleasant weekend. It being five o'clock, I do now leave the Chair until eleven o'clock Monday morning.
At 1.01 p.m. the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.
